chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
Two types of insurance protect your purchase from different angles: home insurance (against damage and loss) and title insurance (against legal problems tied to the property). Understanding them means avoiding costly gaps in coverage.

This guide explains both, what they cover, and why they matter.

Informational content. Each chapter ends with a lined “My Notes” page.

chapters.title: Home Insurance
chapters.objective: Protecting the building and your belongings.
chapters.html:
Protecting the building and your belongings.

Home insurance covers your property and belongings against risks such as fire, water damage, and theft, and includes civil liability. It must be in force as of the possession date — lenders require it.

  • Check the coverage, exclusions, and deductibles.
  • Certain situations (oil tank, aging roof, flood-prone area) affect insurability and the premium.
  • In a co-ownership, the syndicate's insurance covers the building; you insure your belongings and improvements.
Émilie's tip

Obtain your home insurance BEFORE signing: it must be active on the possession date. A number of properties (old tank, roof nearing end of life) are harder to insure, so check early.

chapters.title: Title Insurance
chapters.html:
Protecting yourself against legal problems.

Title insurance protects against certain problems related to the property title: title defects, encroachment, non-compliance, fraud, or an irregularity that may have gone undetected. It can sometimes replace or supplement a recent certificate of location, depending on the case.

It's a one-time protection (single premium) often offered by the notary. It does not replace home insurance.

Émilie's tip

Title insurance is an inexpensive legal safety net. Discuss it with your notary: in certain situations, it can simplify the transaction and protect you from an unforeseen title problem.

chapters.title: Covering Yourself Well Without Gaps
chapters.html:
Combining protections wisely.

  • Home: damage, loss, and liability (mandatory for the lender).
  • Title: legal ownership problems (optional but useful).
  • Make sure no significant risk is left uncovered.
  • Reassess your insurance after major renovations.

Two complementary protections, two kinds of peace of mind.

Émilie's tip

Take stock once a year and after every major renovation: a value that rises without adjusted coverage is a silent risk.

chapters.title: Action Plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, in concrete terms.

This week

  1. Get a home insurance quote.
  2. Check for anything that complicates insurability.

Within 30 days

  1. Discuss title insurance with the notary.
  2. Make sure there are no coverage gaps.

After that

  1. Reassess your insurance after renovations.

chapters.title: Resources & Glossary
chapters.html:
• Home insurance: covers damage, loss, and liability; mandatory for the lender.
  • Title insurance: covers legal problems tied to the property.
  • Deductible: the amount you pay out of pocket on a claim.
  • Insurability: how easily a property can be insured, based on its condition and risks.
  • Civil liability: protection if you cause damage to others.
